chapter.title: Socrates and the habit of asking why

cards.body:
Back at the long dinner table, one guest never states an opinion. He is barefoot, snub-nosed, and he only asks. Someone says "cheating is bad," and he leans in: "What do you mean by cheating?" Then, "Why is that bad?" Then again.

Every guest who has sat down since, for about 2,400 years, has had to answer his questions first. His one idea: **a belief is only as solid as the answer underneath it.**
cards.simpler: Picture a long dinner table. One guest never shares his own view. He is barefoot, has a snub nose, and only asks questions. Someone says cheating is bad. He leans in and asks what they mean by cheating, then why it is bad, then why again. For about 2,400 years, every guest since has had to answer him first. His one idea: **a belief is only as solid as the answer underneath it.**

cards.prompt: Your friend Priya says "Lying is always wrong." You ask why. "Because it hurts people." You ask, "What about a lie that hurts nobody?" Priya goes quiet. What just happened?

options.text: Priya lost. Her belief was false.
Priya found the edge of her reasons. That's where the thinking starts.

whyNot.a: That's a verdict, not a finding: running out of reasons shows the belief needs more support, not that it is false.
whyNot.c: That's manners, not method: the question was fair, and the pause is useful, not an injury.

cards.reteach: Asking "why" of an answer, then "why" of that answer, is like tapping a floorboard to see if it's hollow. When Priya goes quiet, you have not proven her wrong. You have found the exact spot where her reasons stop, which is the only spot worth thinking about.

cards.title: The man who only asked
cards.body:
Around 400 BC, in Athens, a stonemason's son named Socrates spent his days in the market asking people who claimed to know something to define it. A general on courage. A priest on holiness. He wrote nothing down. What we have is his student Plato writing the conversations later.

The move is simple. Take a belief. Ask "what do you mean?" or "why?" Take the answer and ask again. Within 3 to 5 rounds the person either finds a solid floor or finds they were standing on air.

This is the *Socratic method*: **testing a belief by questioning it until the answers run out.**
cards.simpler: Around 400 BC in Athens, a stonemason's son named Socrates spent his days in the market. He found people who claimed to know something and asked them to explain it. A general on courage. A priest on holiness. He wrote nothing down. His student Plato recorded the talks later. The move is easy. Take a belief. Ask what it means, or why. Ask again about the answer. After 3 to 5 rounds, the person finds solid ground or finds nothing under their feet. That is the Socratic method: **testing a belief by questioning it until the answers run out.**

cards.title: Euthyphro is late for something
cards.body:
On the courthouse steps, Socrates meets a man called Euthyphro, who is prosecuting his own father for letting a worker die. Socrates is impressed: you must know exactly what holiness is, then. "Yes. It's doing what I'm doing." That's an example, not a definition. "Fine. Holiness is what the gods love." But the gods disagree with each other, so the same act would be holy and unholy at once.

Five rounds later, Euthyphro remembers he is late for something and leaves. Plato wrote it down. **Nobody has ever been late for something quite so conveniently.**
cards.simpler: On the courthouse steps, Socrates meets a man named Euthyphro. He is taking his own father to court for letting a worker die. Socrates says he must know exactly what holiness is, then. Euthyphro says yes, it is what he is doing. That is an example, not a meaning. He tries again: holiness is what the gods love. But the gods disagree, so one act would be holy and unholy at once. Five rounds later, Euthyphro remembers he is late and leaves. **Nobody has ever been late for something quite so conveniently.**

cards.prompt: Your cousin Arjun says, "Hard work always pays off." Which reply is the Socratic move?

options.text: "No it doesn't. Uncle Ravi worked hard for 30 years and got nothing."
"What do you mean by 'pays off'? Money, or something else?"
"True. That's why I'm at my desk at 6am."

whyNot.a: That's a counter-claim from chapter 1, not a question: you've replaced his belief with yours instead of testing his.
whyNot.c: That's agreement, not testing: nothing under the belief has been tapped.

cards.reteach: The Socratic move never adds a new opinion to the table. It asks the speaker to say what they mean, then asks why that is so, and keeps going. Arguing back or agreeing both skip the step where Arjun has to look under his own words.

cards.title: Why it killed him, and how to use it on yourself
cards.body:
In 399 BC Athens put Socrates on trial for not honouring the city's gods and for corrupting the young. A jury of several hundred citizens found him guilty. He was given poison hemlock and drank it. At the trial, as Plato tells it, he said the unexamined life is not worth living. Asking "why" in public had made too many important people look hollow.

Now turn it inward. Pick one belief you hold. Ask why. Answer honestly. Ask why of that answer. Go 5 deep.

**Where you say "it just is" or "everyone knows," stop and mark the spot.** That is not failure. It is a map of where to think next.
cards.simpler: In 399 BC, Athens put Socrates on trial for not honouring the city's gods and for leading young people astray. A jury of several hundred found him guilty. He drank poison hemlock and died. At the trial, Plato says, he claimed a life without questions is not worth living. Asking why in public had made too many powerful people look empty. Now point it at yourself. Pick one belief. Ask why. Answer honestly. Ask why again. Go 5 deep. **Where you say "it just is" or "everyone knows," stop and mark the spot.** That is not failure. It is a map of where to think next.

cards.body:
Dev tried the method on his flatmate during a row about dishes. "Why do you think that? And why that? And why that?" He already knew the answer he wanted her to reach. That is cross-examination, not Socrates.

How to spot it: **if you could not be surprised by the answer, you are not asking a real question.** Socrates asked questions he could not answer either.
cards.simpler: Dev tried this on his flatmate during a fight about dishes. Why do you think that? And why that? And why that? But he already knew the answer he wanted her to reach. That is like a lawyer grilling a witness, not Socrates. Here is the test: **if you could not be surprised by the answer, you are not asking a real question.** Socrates asked questions he could not answer himself.

cards.prompt: You ask yourself why 5 times about "I should always reply to messages fast" and land on "I just feel it's true." What does that spot tell you?

options.text: The belief is false. Drop it.
Your reasons end here. This is the place to look next.
You picked the wrong belief. Start over with another.

whyNot.a: That's a verdict, not a finding: a belief with thin reasons might still be right, it just isn't held up yet.
whyNot.c: That's dodging, not method: hitting the floor is the point of the exercise, not a sign you chose badly.

cards.reteach: The method does not tell you whether a belief is true. It tells you where your reasons stop. Hitting "I just feel it" on round 5 is the method working exactly as Socrates used it: now you know which belief is standing on air, and you can go find it a floor.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Socrates asked "what do you mean?" and "why?" until people's reasons ran out, and Athens executed him for it in 399 BC. **Do the same to your own beliefs, 5 whys deep, and the spot where you stop is where real thinking starts.**
cards.simpler: Socrates asked people what they meant and why, over and over, until their reasons ran out. Athens put him to death for it in 399 BC. Try the same thing on your own beliefs. **Ask why 5 times in a row, and the place where you get stuck is where real thinking begins.** That stuck spot is not a dead end. It is the start of the work.

cards.body: Tonight, in your notes app: write one belief you hold. Under it, write "why?" and answer. Ask why of that answer. Five rows. Mark the row where you ran out.
cards.simpler: Tonight, open your notes app. Write down one thing you believe. Under it, write the word why, and answer it. Then ask why about that answer. Keep going until you have five rows. Mark the row where you ran out of answers. **That marked row is where your real thinking starts.** It takes five minutes and shows you where your belief rests on solid ground and where it does not.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now ask 5 'why' questions in a row about a belief you hold and notice where your answers run out.
